title: Automate expense categorization
description: A system that checks every transaction against your chart of accounts and flags anything it isn't confident about.

api.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
api.content: A way for two programs to talk to each other. When a tool says 'connect via API,' it means software can send requests and get data back automatically — no manual copy-paste needed.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

batch-api.title: Batch API
batch-api.content: A way to send a big pile of requests to Claude at once and get the results back later (usually within 24 hours) at a discount. Good for one-time bulk jobs like classifying 10,000 customer support tickets.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: A [batch](#tooltip-batch-api) of receipts or a bank export lands, and this system assigns every transaction a GL code or spend category, with the reasoning attached so a human can spot-check the uncertain ones. AI-based capture now reaches 95%+ field-level accuracy on document data extraction, versus 1-4% error rates in manual entry, per [Ardent Partners' AP metrics research](https://ardentpartners.com/ap-metrics-that-matter-in-2025/).

Categorization only holds up when the model shows its reasoning per line item, so a mistake surfaces before it hits the books. The system is only as good as the chart of accounts and prior categorization rules it's given.

Run it as a weekly paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) against a statement export, a saved skill, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that pulls each new batch through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors). Every version holds its output for review before anything posts to your books.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming where your transactions come from, your chart of accounts, which categories are genuinely ambiguous, and who reviews the output before it's final.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that categorizes my expenses against my chart of accounts every time I export transactions. Ask me questions, one at a time, about where my transaction data comes from, what my GL codes or categories are, which categorizations are ambiguous or contested, who reviews the output before it's final, and how I want exceptions flagged. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces the edge cases your chart of accounts doesn't already cover, and the scope document becomes the brief for every build session after it.

items: Where your transaction data lives, and whether it needs cleanup before the AI sees it.
Whether your chart of accounts already has enough example-based rules, or whether you need to write those first.
Who does the final review pass and how often, before this turns into trusting the AI blindly.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are your accounting software (QuickBooks, Xero, and NetSuite publish official [API](#tooltip-api) docs), your card or expense platform, and a spreadsheet for the review layer. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real batch of transactions. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Categorize this batch of transactions against my chart of accounts and flag anything you're not confident about.

Context: Transaction export attached (CSV with date, vendor, amount, memo). My chart of accounts and category rules are [paste or attach: your GL code list with examples of past categorizations]. Recurring vendors that always map to one category: [list them, e.g. "AWS -> Software", "Delta -> Travel"].

Rules: Assign one GL code per transaction. If a transaction could reasonably fit more than one code, flag it instead of guessing and explain the ambiguity. Never invent a GL code that isn't in my chart of accounts. Flag any transaction over [$ threshold] regardless of confidence, for manual review.

Output format: A table with columns Date, Vendor, Amount, Assigned GL Code, Confidence (high/medium/low), Reasoning. A second table listing only the flagged/low-confidence rows.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the recurring vendors up front cuts the ambiguous pile down to the transactions that need a human look.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. One GL code per row, ambiguous ones flagged with reasoning, nothing invented outside your chart of accounts?
**Feedback.** Correct the underlying rule so the same vendor doesn't get miscoded next batch.

items: Add OCR so photographed receipts feed in directly.
Build a monthly summary of spend by category on top of the categorized data.
Add a rule that routes anything above a dollar threshold to a manager for approval before posting.
Track categorization accuracy over time and retrain the rules on your corrections.

children.text: **Measure** against a written [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each categorized batch, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, transactions categorized, transactions flagged as ambiguous, corrections I made, and which GL code got fixed most. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a chronically miscoded vendor visible after a few batches.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few batches straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A model will confidently assign a plausible-sounding code even when a transaction is genuinely ambiguous, so every categorization needs a visible confidence signal alongside the answer. Never let categorized output post to the ledger without a human review step first.
